Chapter Twenty-Four: The Four Noble Truths (Ten Volumes). Chapter Twenty-Four: The Four Noble Truths.
The reason this chapter appears is that wherever there is a mind that grasps at attainment, there will necessarily be dependence and attachment. Regarding the preceding two [chapters]...
In the eleventh chapter, "Establishing the Worldly Dharmas of Humans," the Master of the Treatise sought them but found no source;
he therefore cited the supramundane Tathāgata as proof that the world exists.
Next, when seeking the supramundane Tathāgata, one does not find him;
thus, one cites the mundane inversions as proof that the supramundane exists.
When seeking the mundane inversions in their superior form, one does not find them.
The opponent says:
"If that were so, there would be neither mundane nor supramundane realms at all.
Yet, in reality, there are the Four Noble Truths."
Consequently, there must be both the mundane and the supramundane.
Thus, the two truths of suffering and its origin are mundane,
while the two truths of cessation and the path are termed supramundane.
Therefore, it should not be that there is neither the mundane nor the supramundane.
Now, observing that the Four Noble Truths cannot be apprehended,
the aforementioned point— that there is neither the mundane nor the supramundane— is established.
Since it is neither mundane nor supramundane, it is precisely the Middle Way;
thus, when contemplation is developed within the causal stage, this conceptual proliferation is extinguished.
Second, the outsider says:
Perversion is that from which the Tathāgata is free;
the Four Noble Truths are that which the Tathāgata has realized,
and they are also that which the Tathāgata has taught.
Throughout the Tathāgata’s single period of appearing in the world, though the beginning and end differ, they equally clarify the Four Noble Truths. Therefore,
from the initial turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths,
up until the teaching on the joy of the mind at the time of Nirvāṇa, it is thus.
The reason why the Four Noble Truths are elucidated at both the beginning and the end is that the Four Noble Truths are the foundation of both delusion and awakening; to be deluded by them,
the six realms of existence fall into chaotic confusion.
Upon awakening to this, there are the worthies and sages of the three vehicles;
therefore, from beginning to end, the four truths are clarified.
If this were so, there would be no distinction between the mundane and the supramundane.
Third, as for those that arise from the category of inversion (*viparyāsa*):
inversion is the delusive affliction that causes confusion,
while the Four Truths are the objects of that confusion.
By seeing the Four Truths, one destroys the four inversions; therefore,
while previously one sought the obstructing agent and found it to have no source,
now one examines that which was deluded and finds it cannot be obtained.
Therefore, this chapter exists.
However, the Four Noble Truths are of two kinds:
first, those that are finite (measurable).
The two immeasurables.
The fruits of suffering within the three realms are called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).
The karma and afflictions that induce the suffering of the three realms are called the Truth of Origination (*samudayasatya*).
Unconditioned nirvana is called the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
That which remedies these afflictions is called the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). This [set] is finite.
Regarding the four noble truths with their finite measures, the various masters of the Hīnayāna treatises differ.
The *Vibhāṣā* states: "The *Abhidharma* teachers say that the five aggregates of clinging (*pañcopādānaskandha*) as suffering are called the truth of suffering."
The cause of the outflows is the truth of origination;
analytical cessation is the truth of cessation;
and the states of training and beyond-training are the truth of the path.
The Dṛṣṭāntavādins say:
Name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is the truth of suffering (duḥkhasatya);
the fetters and karma are the truth of origination (samudayasatya).
The cessation of fetters and karma is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
tranquility (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) are the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*). The Vibhajyavādins say:
The eight sufferings are suffering; they constitute the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkha-satya*).
Other forms of suffering, though indeed painful, do not constitute the Truth of Suffering.
That which brings about craving for the future is the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*).
Although other forms of craving and other contaminated phenomena (*sāsrava-dharma*) are indeed accumulation (*samudaya*), they are not the Truth of Accumulation (*samudaya-satya*).
The exhaustion of craving for future existence is cessation (*nirodha*) and is the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*);
however, the exhaustion of other forms of craving and other contaminated phenomena is not the Truth of Cessation.
The Eightfold Right Path is the Truth of the Path;
other dharmas of training (śaikṣa) and all dharmas beyond training (aśaikṣa) are not the Truth of the Path.
Question: Do these four truths encompass all dharmas exhaustively?
Answer: Space and analytical cessation (apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha) are not included within the Four Noble Truths.
The Four Noble Truths are established based on attraction and aversion;
since those two [space and cessation] do not involve aversion, they are neither suffering nor its origin.
Because they are not objects of delight, they are neither the cessation nor the path.
Furthermore, because these two are untainted (*anāsrava*), they are neither suffering nor its origin;
because they are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*), they are neither cessation nor the path.
Furthermore, the four truths are established based on cause and effect;
since those [other phenomena] are neither cause nor effect, they are not truths.
Question: What is meant by "truth" (satya)?
The answer consists of two points:
first, it is truly suffering;
second, because it gives rise to non-perverted understanding, it is called a truth (*satya*).
Question: What is meant by "Noble Truth"?
Answer: It is called a Noble Truth because it is that which is realized by the noble ones.
Furthermore, in the past, there was an ordinary person who debated the truths with a sage.
The ordinary person said,
"There exist permanence, bliss, self, and purity."
The Sage said,
"Go together to the Buddha's presence to have it resolved.
The Buddha said:
As it is known by the noble ones (ārya),
these are called "Noble Truths" (āryasatya) because the noble ones have realized these truths through the cessation of dispute.
The Sāṃkhya school understands only that which is finite (parimāṇavat).
However, their meanings differ:
the *Shu* (Abhidharmakośa) clarifies that suffering pervades the three aggregates (*skandha*),
whereas the *Cheng lun* (Satyasiddhi-śāstra) holds it to be only the mind.
The discourse on suffering encompasses both the outflowing (*sāsrava*) and the non-outflowing (*anāsrava*); however, the enumeration refers only to the outflowing.
The enumeration of the origin (*samudaya*) encompasses all three aggregates (*skandha*).
The *Abhidharmakośa-śāstra* takes only karma and afflictions as causes;
because they accumulate and provide conditions for existence, they are the fruit that recompenses the past,
while their arising in the subsequent moment serves as the cause.
Only that which has the capacity to produce [suffering] belongs to the category of origination (*samudaya*); that which is produced is suffering (*duḥkha*).
According to the *Abhidharmakośa*, this very capacity to produce is itself a retribution of suffering.
The anger of a venomous snake is a phenomenon subject to retribution; this is called the Truth of Suffering (*duḥkhasatya*).

As for the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*), it refers exclusively to the extinction of the afflictions (*kleśa*); the cessation of untainted phenomena (*anāsravadharma*) is not the Truth of Cessation.
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* explains that untainted cessation (*anāsrava-nirodha*) is also the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The *Abhidharmakośa* explains that the permanent suppression of the fetters (*saṃyojana*) within the path of preparation (*prayoga-mārga*) is non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* further explains that the cessation [attained] within the five stages of preparation is also the truth of cessation.
The *Abhidharmakośa* clarifies that all untainted (*anāsrava*) formations are the Truth of the Path (*mārgasatya*),
excluding those that merely resemble them.
The *Satyasiddhi-śāstra*, however, clarifies that both the real and the similar are the Truth of the Path.
The *Śāriputrābhidharma* clarifies that there are dharmas not subject to guidance;
the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* clarifies that there is a mind subject to guidance.
Next, regarding the four truths of the immeasurables: the two types of birth and death constitute suffering.
The five abodes constitute the origin (*samudaya*).
The cessation of the two deaths and the five abodes constitutes cessation (*nirodha*).
The true understanding that remedies the delusions of these five abodes constitutes the truth of the path (*mārga-satya*).
Furthermore, that which is measured and immeasurable is also called "that which is made" and "that which is not made.
Even after there has been that which is measured, there is still that which is produced;
for example, after the suffering of fragmentation, the suffering of transformation can still be observed.
It is called "with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*).
Because there is no further suffering to be perceived after the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkha*),
it is called "without effort" (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The same applies to the other three [truths].
Now, regarding the statement "destroying the Four Truths":
first, it refers to destroying those who study the Mahāyāna by claiming that the Four Truths do not exist.
Second, there are those who destroy the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), asserting that the Four Noble Truths are substantially existent (*svabhāva-sat*).
These two categories encompass all delusions;
now, their respective understandings are refuted.
Therefore, it is said that they refute the Four Noble Truths.
The reason for this is that followers of the Mahāyāna deny the existence of the Four Noble Truths.
This destroys the meaning of the Buddha’s Four Noble Truths.
Those of the Hīnayāna who reckon that intrinsic nature exists also destroy the Four Noble Truths.
Furthermore, there are two other types of persons who destroy the meaning of the Four Noble Truths.
The first refers to the proponent of the treatise who, by adhering to emptiness, subverts the Four Noble Truths;
the second refers to those who, by adhering to the intrinsic existence of phenomena, subvert the Four Noble Truths.
Both of these are followers of the Hīnayāna; however,
because they claim there is both the refutation by another and the establishment by oneself,
they constitute two types.
Now, these two points are refuted;
therefore, it is said that the Four Noble Truths are refuted. Furthermore, this demonstrates that both of these individuals do not understand the Buddha’s teachings on the Great and Small Vehicles.
Those of the Hīnayāna do not understand that the Buddha’s dependent origination possesses the nature of existence.
Those of the Mahāyāna who do not understand the emptiness of the Buddha’s Mahāyāna fall into a perverted emptiness.
Having become confused regarding both the Great and Small Vehicles, they are equally deluded about the two truths.
The Master, his clear wisdom fully internalized and the wind of his compassion fanning outward, [composed this work].
To rescue those of both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles,
he refutes their dual delusions and clarifies that there is neither such emptiness nor existence;
thus it is said that "neither empty nor existent" is precisely the Middle Way of true reality.
As for "the reality within," there is in truth no such thing as existence or non-existence.
This refers precisely to the Buddha’s teaching that existence and non-existence are merely conventional designations established through dependent origination.
The Middle Way exists by way of conventional designation;
as it says below,
this too is a conventional designation.
This is also the Middle Way.
Furthermore, it refutes these notions of "large" and "small," clarifying that such large and small do not exist.
Within this, the actual directions are merely conventional designations (*prajñapti*) for "large" and "small" based on causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*).
That is to say, it is by depending on these conventional designations of large and small that consciousness perceives the path as having never been large or small.

Furthermore, if one examines the overall intent of the treatise from the beginning to the end—from the "Chapter on Causes and Conditions" (*Hetu-pratyaya-varga*) up to just before the "Four Noble Truths" (*Catvāri-āryasatyāni*)—it is evident.
The opponent maintains the existence [of things] and challenges the proponent.
At the beginning of this chapter, the opponent maintains emptiness and challenges the proponent.
This initial challenge based on the existence [of things] reveals that the opponent does not understand emptiness.
Now, to maintain that emptiness makes it difficult to clarify that outsiders do not recognize existence is to be confused about the two truths.
This is also the initial objection raised by a follower of the Hīnayāna against the Master of the Treatise.
Now, by maintaining that the Mahāyāna is difficult [to understand], one challenges the proponent of the treatise,
thereby revealing that the outsider does not recognize the distinction between the Great and Small Vehicles.
Furthermore, from the beginning, by maintaining that intrinsic nature exists, one challenges the proponent of the treatise.
This reveals that outsiders, failing to understand dependent origination, now cling to a false emptiness and challenge the Master.
It further shows that these outsiders do not recognize authentic emptiness;
the Master, out of compassion for such deluded beings, addresses them.
Therefore, having refuted this [notion of] emptiness and existence by clarifying that such emptiness and existence do not ultimately exist,
he subsequently sets forth the emptiness and existence of the two truths according to causes and conditions.
Furthermore, this reveals that the opponent has thus far maintained the position of existence to challenge the Proponent.
If one does not rely on emptiness, the objection is not established as an objection.
Now, since you who uphold emptiness object by grasping at the characteristics of emptiness,
your objection is likewise not established as an objection.
If one holds that the nature of things is empty, the objection is not established;
if one holds that the nature of things exists, the response is not established.
Why is it that, in this chapter, the emptiness and existence of both externalists are refuted in order to clarify the Four Noble Truths?
Answer: From the very beginning of our own treatise, we have refuted either the mundane alone or the supramundane alone;
however, since the Four Noble Truths comprehensively encompass both the mundane and the supramundane, [the refutation applies to both].
Since this constitutes the great core of the Buddha-dharma, this chapter clarifies how the externalist views of both emptiness and existence are refuted regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Question: Does the Master [Nāgārjuna] himself maintain the Four Noble Truths?

Answer: The Master of the Treatise has never asserted that there are four, nor has he ever asserted that there are not four, nor that it is both four and not four, nor that it is neither four nor not four.
Thus, the *Dharmapada* states:
The true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is where mental activity and verbal expression cease.
Question: Since the Master has never maintained that there are four or not four, for what reason do the Buddhist sūtras speak of the Four Noble Truths?
Answer: Although they are neither four nor not-four, for the sake of sentient beings as a skillful means, the Buddhas speak of them as four and not-four.
Therefore, the following verse says:
"The Buddhas rely upon the two truths to preach the Dharma for sentient beings."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Although sentient beings cannot be apprehended within the two truths,
the bodhisattva dwells within the two truths and preaches the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings."
The Commentary states:
"For those who cling to existence, one teaches emptiness;
for those who cling to emptiness, one teaches existence."
It is the same now:
for those who are attached to the existence of the four [noble truths], he teaches that there are no four;
for those who are attached to the non-existence of the four, he clarifies that there are the four truths.
In the ultimate discussion of all phenomena, they have never been either four or not four.
This chapter is divided into two parts.
First, the opponent’s critique that the Master’s adherence to emptiness constitutes a commonality with them.
Second, the author of the treatise refutes the externalist's attachment to the existence of conditioned phenomena in common;
this is done by employing the externalist's own position to refute the view of emptiness,
thereby quelling the nihilistic mind of those who cling to their teachings.
Regarding the Master’s refutation of existence, this is intended to eliminate the common misconception of sentient beings.
Since the Four Noble Truths constitute the great mainstay of the Buddha-dharma and fully encompass both mundane and supramundane phenomena.
Therefore, this chapter refutes the views of annihilationism and eternalism to reveal the Middle Way,
thereby inducing contemplation within the causal stage. Furthermore,
regarding the opponent’s errors, the Master’s critique is further divided into two parts.
There are two parts: the prose and the verses.
The prose may have two meanings.
First, it arises from the Chapter on Perversion.
Next follows the reason for the Chapter on the Four Truths:
secondly, because [the opponent] intends to refute the Master’s [Vasubandhu’s] doctrine of emptiness,
he first establishes the meaning of the Four Truths.
The verse is divided into two parts:
the first part demonstrates that the proponent’s position results in the non-existence of the Four Noble Truths, the Three Jewels, and supramundane dharmas;
the second part demonstrates that it results in the non-existence of cause and effect, sin and merit, and mundane dharmas.
The first section also has two parts.
The first half cites the Master’s position that [things] are empty, beginning with the words:
"In this way, there would be no... and so forth.
The second part raises objections against the proponent of the treatise,
which is further divided into two sections;
the first clarifies that the Four Noble Truths do not exist.
Next, the non-existence of the Three Jewels is explained.
Because there is no arising, there is neither suffering nor its origin;
for suffering is that which is produced, while the origin is that which produces it.
Because there is no cessation, there is no path to cessation.
The Truth of the Path is that which can bring about cessation; when cessation is reached, it constitutes the Truth of Cessation.
Since there is no cessation,
how can there be a path to cessation?
Because the Four Noble Truths do not exist, the second section below clarifies that the Three Jewels do not exist.
Furthermore, two distinct sections are opened:
first, a specific explanation of the absence of the Three Jewels;
second, half a verse summarizing the absence of the Three.
The absence of the three [jewels] is explained separately as being three distinct absences.
Within the absence of the Jewel of the Saṃgha, this is further divided into two parts;
the first two verses specifically explain the absence of the Saṃgha.
The subsequent half-verse summarizes the absence of the Sangha.
These two verses are divided into two parts;
the first verse clarifies the absence of the four practices.
The following verse distinguishes the absence of those who are heading toward the fruit;
the text is easily understood.
Furthermore, the first verse lacks the objective realm of the Four Noble Truths.
The next verse lacks the wisdom regarding the Four Noble Truths;
the third verse proceeds to clarify the absence of the Jewel of the Sangha.
This interpretation is excellent and should be followed.
Later, the Master returns the critique to the opponent and likewise makes this same distinction.
This occurs below the section beginning with "The dharma of emptiness destroys cause and effect."
The second fault is that the Master of Treatises, by adhering to emptiness, incurs the error of negating cause and effect, as well as sin and merit.
It was previously clarified that the Four Truths do not exist;
thus, [the opponent’s position] generally subverts both mundane and supramundane causes and effects, including the Three Jewels.
Why is this explained again now?
The answer is that there are generally three reasons.
First, what has been clarified above concerns those who cling to emptiness.
From the Buddha’s departure for the Deer Park and his teaching of the Four Truths and the Three Jewels,
up to the instruction at the Twin Śāla Trees—
now it is clarified that there was no Buddha when he first attained the Way.
For the sake of Trapusa and others, he taught the causes and effects, merits and faults, pertaining to humans and devas;
therefore, those who cling to emptiness completely subvert the teachings of the five vehicles.
Second, it was clarified above that there are no internal dharmas of cause, effect, merit, or fault.
Now it is clarified that there are no external dharmas of cause and effect, sin and merit— namely,
the worldly virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety,
and wisdom. Thirdly, the foregoing has clarified the absence of objects of sin and merit.
Now, it is clarified that there are no such things as sin, merit, or the Three Jewels.
The Four Noble Truths are the realm of sin and merit;
by believing in them, one generates merit.
To slander it brings about sin.
The response consists of thirty-four verses,
which are broadly divided into three sections.
The first thirteen lines clarify that the opponent is deluded regarding emptiness.
The following section, from "As for the faults you have attributed to the dharma of emptiness," constitutes the second part, which refutes the opponent’s attachment to existence.
The final two lines, beginning with "If there were no emptiness," constitute the third part, which provides both a warning and an exhortation.
He exhorts them to abandon the view of a fixed nature and emptiness, and encourages their study of dependent origination.
This section consists of two parts.
First, it clarifies how external opponents, being deluded regarding emptiness, perversely raise erroneous objections.
Regarding your claim that I am attached to emptiness, the second section below clarifies that the Master has realized emptiness; therefore, there is no fault.
This section consists of four parts, each with four sub-sections.
In the first part, the four sub-sections are as follows: first, it clarifies how outsiders fail to understand the three dharmas and thus arbitrarily raise doubts and objections.
The second clarifies how outsiders, failing to recognize two dharmas, give rise to perverse objections.
The third recounts how outsiders, failing to understand one dharma, give rise to perverse objections.
The fourth [reason] is that, failing to understand the three preceding gates,
they cling dogmatically to a single dharma with a fixed nature;
this obstructs the Buddha from being able to preach the Mahāyāna earlier.
Question: For what reason is it stated that the outsider does not understand the three dharmas?
Answer: Generally, when one wishes to answer an external question, one must first discern whether it is a valid question or not;
here, it is stated that the outsider does not comprehend these three dharmas.
To raise a question by way of doubt is not to pose a question at all;
it is, in fact, to provide an answer.
First, it clarifies those who do not understand the three dharmas.
First, not knowing emptiness:
although followers of the Hīnayāna realize the emptiness of persons,
they cling to all phenomena as being existent and thus do not know that their fundamental nature is empty.
Regarding the causes and conditions for the two kinds of emptiness:
it is said that the Buddha taught emptiness with the intention of treating those who have the disease of [clinging to] existence; therefore, he taught emptiness.
Furthermore, if one is attached to emptiness, one is not transformed by the Buddha.
As for the meaning of the three kinds of emptiness, outsiders do not understand how to abide in this emptiness;
the Buddha taught that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is emptiness.
It is not said that conventional truth is also empty.
You should not, upon hearing of emptiness, conclude that cause and effect, as well as sin and merit, are lost.
Therefore, the "Chapter on Causes and Conditions" states:
If all things were ultimately empty, how could there be retribution for sins and merits?
In that case, the Two Truths would not exist.
Furthermore, the meaning of emptiness is explained as teaching emptiness in order to clarify non-emptiness.
Therefore, it is said below:
"Emptiness is also empty.
Because you cling to and grasp at the characteristics of emptiness, you do not understand the true meaning of emptiness.
Below the passage "The Buddhas rely on the two truths," the second section clarifies that outsiders do not understand these two dharmas,
and thus they raise erroneous objections.
Because they do not know that what is manifest is actually non-existent,
they do not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
They do not know that although it is non-existent, it is nonetheless manifest as existent.
Therefore, not understanding conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), one raises the aforementioned false objection.
[The opponent] asks: "At what point does the outsider lose the two truths?"

Answer: From the beginning of the treatise up until the section on the Four Noble Truths, [the opponent] clings to the view that all phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature and does not believe in ultimate emptiness;
therefore, they do not know the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
From the Chapter on the Four Truths, they cling to ultimate emptiness,
asserting that the Three Jewels and the Four Truths do not exist;
thus, they fail to understand conventional truth while yet proceeding to discourse upon the two truths.
This passage returns to explain and establish the three dharmas mentioned above.
As for the statement "one who does not know emptiness," it means one who does not know that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is empty by its very nature.
Regarding the condition of emptiness:
the Buddhas, abiding within the two truths,
preach the Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
For those attached to existence, he teaches emptiness;
for those attached to emptiness, he teaches existence.
The meaning of emptiness is precisely the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
It is not that conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is empty.
Furthermore, regarding the presentation of the two truths: the opponent, by clinging to emptiness, loses conventional truth;
having lost conventional truth, they also lose the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
As explained in the "Chapter on Causality" (Pratyaya-parivarta),
we now clarify that there are two truths in order to counter those outsiders who do not accept the existence of the two truths.
Therefore, the present text describes the two truths.
Furthermore, by recounting the exposition of the two truths, the Master himself avoids the fault [of inconsistency], stating:
"I maintain the doctrine of the two truths."
In the ultimate sense (*paramārtha*), emptiness is devoid of the Three Jewels;
in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*), however, the Three Jewels do exist.
If you raise an objection from the standpoint of the ultimate sense, you will instead establish my own position.
If you challenge me on the basis of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), yet conventional truth possesses the Three Jewels,
how can you then raise the objection that there are no Three Jewels? Furthermore,
this explains the intended meaning of the two truths.
The preceding clarification of emptiness means that the phenomena of cause and effect as you perceive them do not exist;
therefore, it is said they are "non-existent.
It does not mean that the Buddha-dharma, its causes and conditions, and the two truths do not exist.
Furthermore, this chapter elucidates the Four Truths.
Since the Two Truths are a category within the Truths,
it elucidates the Two Truths.
These three verses are further divided into three distinct sections.
The first verse clarifies that the Master of the Treatise, relying on the two truths, expounds the Dharma for the Buddha;
therefore, there is no superior fault.
The second verse clarifies that outsiders do not understand the two truths;
therefore, they fall into error regarding both emptiness and existence.
The third verse clarifies the resolution of doubts and difficulties.
The first half of the verse correctly explains that the Buddha teaches the Dharma by relying on the two truths;
the second half enumerates the names of these two truths.
Question: For what reason is it said that the Buddha teaches the Dharma by relying on the two truths?
Answer: If one speaks of the Dharma based on conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya), then the Three Jewels and the Four Noble Truths remain perfectly intact;
therefore, there is no supreme fault.
This demonstrates that the opponent, not understanding conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), has groundlessly raised these objections;
for I have been explaining the Dharma based on ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Thus far, I have clarified that all things are empty.
This immediately reveals that the externalist’s adherence to the existence of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) fails to accord with the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
Question: In what sense is it said to be based on the meaning of the two truths?
Answer: Because both emptiness and existence, as understood by ordinary beings and noble ones respectively, are real, they are called the two truths.
Because all that is spoken is based on these two realities, everything taught is true;
thus it is said that "it is taught in reliance upon the two truths.
Question: What are these two truths?
What is the truth of the teaching?
The answer is: that which is relied upon consists of the two truths.
Because they are both real for both ordinary beings and noble ones, they are called the two truths.
Furthermore, regarding the two truths, it means that form has never been either empty or existent;
since these two understandings are real,
it is said that "the two are the truths."
The *Śata-śāstra* cites dates, pears, and melons, all of which are not empty;
the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* cites the shape of the ring finger and the name of the index finger, both of which are real.
That which serves as the basis for reliance is precisely the truth of the teaching (*deśanā-satya*).
The Buddha preaches the Dharma for sentient beings based on these two truths;
all are words of sincere truth,
and are therefore called "real."
Question: Is there a difference regarding that which depends [upon it]?
Answer: From the perspective of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), this is spoken as the true reality;
from the perspective of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), this is spoken as a skillful means (*upāya*) according to what is appropriate.
Question: It is said that the teachings concerning humans, devas, and the two vehicles are provisional teachings (*upāya-deśanā*).
Now, you speak of the human dharma and so forth within the Mahāyāna.
How is it that all teachings spoken according to worldly convention are considered provisional?

Answer: Because the feeling of equanimity lacks the two preceding types of suffering, it possesses only the suffering of conditioned existence.
Therefore, we speak of the general [suffering] by way of its specific [aspects].
Second, even granting that you have both the general and specific six types of suffering, impermanence is the basis for two types of suffering:
the suffering of conditioned formations (*saṃskāra-duḥkha*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkha*).
If impermanence existed prior to suffering,
then what would impermanence be employed for?
If impermanence itself were suffering, [then they would be identical].
Furthermore, why is it said that impermanence is the basis for suffering?
If suffering possessed a fixed nature, it would follow that there is no Truth of Cessation; thus [the author] refutes this below.
The Master of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* says:

The remaining two minds are extinguished through remainderless cessation (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirodha*), while the mind of emptiness (*śūnyatā-citta*) is extinguished through remainderless cessation; therefore,
the extinction of these three minds is called the Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
Question: Is it that by destroying existence one attains cessation, or is it that original existence itself ceases?
If it were that original existence ceases, then it would be identical to [the view of] annihilationism.
If the destruction of existence results in the arising of extinction, [one must ask:
since extinction is already inherently present, does it have a cause or is it causeless?
If it were causeless, it would be spontaneous, identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
That which has a cause is impermanent.
Question: According to the Abhidharma, cessation (*nirodha*) is inherently existent. Since suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) possess a fixed nature, [how can they be impermanent]?
Then it would be impossible to extinguish [suffering].
How could one extinguish the accumulation of suffering and attain the extinction that exists by nature?
If there were no Truth of Suffering, there would be no third summary conclusion regarding the Four Noble Truths.
Observing this text, it constitutes a second refutation of the Truth of the Path.
If suffering were definitively possessed of an intrinsic nature, the following second section would revert to the fault of the non-existence of the Three Jewels.
This section consists of two parts according to the text.
The first part generally clarifies the non-existence of the Three Jewels;
the second part specifically clarifies the non-existence of the causes and fruits of the Mahāyāna.
The non-existence of the Three Jewels is further divided into three distinct sections.
Regarding each of the Three Jewels in turn:
first, the absence of the Jewel of the Sangha is explained specifically;
next, the absence of the Jewel of the Sangha is summarized.
The first line of twelve characters clarifies that there are no four [noble] truths.
If one analyzes them as above, this absence of the wisdom of the four truths means that from the four fruits onward, there is no Sangha Jewel.
Question: If you maintain that objects have existed from the beginning, then wisdom must also have existed from the beginning.
If it was not seen originally but is seen now, [how can this be so?]
Furthermore, that which was not an object previously is now an object; yet if it were an object previously, it would also be an object now.
Likewise, that which was not seen previously is not seen now.
If the mind were something that could be cultivated,
then because it would exist through such cultivation,
there would be no need for cultivation now.
Now, since it must be cultivated, one knows that there is no [intrinsic] principle [to be found].
Second, if one refutes it based on what preceded, wisdom originally arises from the object;
since the preceding search for the object was unsuccessful, [wisdom likewise fails].
From what does wisdom arise?
Furthermore, regarding the second point concerning the four fruits, [the opponent] denies that there are four fruits.
If there are no four fruits, then, as for the third point, [the opponent] denies that there are eight noble ones (ārya-pudgala).
Because the Eight Noble Ones do not exist, [the author] returns to the opponent's position below to conclude that the Jewel of the Sangha does not exist.
The next line of verse clarifies the non-existence of the Three Jewels,

Question: The second section below specifically clarifies that there is no Mahāyāna cause or effect.
Now, observing this text, it appears that the term "Mahāyāna" is merely used here in the sense of the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*) within the Śrāvaka vehicle itself.
The preceding question is followed by the subsequent answer.
There are two questions;
the first acknowledges the prior absence.
In the second section of the "Ultimate Path" (niṣṭhā-mārga), the establishment of future existence (punarbhava) is presented;
this establishment is divided into two parts: first, the establishment of the ultimate dharma (paramārtha-dharma).
Because of this path, one is established below as a Perfected Person (*tathāgata*).
In the response, there are two verses divided into two parts;
the first refutes both person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma*).
The second [point] refutes the absence of cause and effect.
The intent of the response is as follows:
Your own establishment of "person" (pudgala) and "dharmas" is not self-evident.
Then you are one who destroys both person and dharma.
In the fourth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, Kātyāyana says:
"First there is the fruit of bodhi; it dispatches wisdom, faith, speech, and body."
"You may cultivate the thirty-two marks to adorn your body;
I shall come later. This is a case where the fruit exists first and the cause is cultivated afterward.
Since the effect already exists beforehand while the cause has not yet arisen,
what kind of effect would it be?
Furthermore, what would be the purpose of cultivating the cause?
Furthermore, since awakening (bodhi) exists prior to the Buddha, your claim that the Buddha does not exist because of awakening is refuted.
Question: This merely refutes the causality of the Hīnayāna.
Does it also refute the Mahāyāna that is characterized by apprehension?
Answer: It primarily refutes the Mahāyāna that is characterized by apprehension, while incidentally refuting the Hīnayāna as well.
Question: How does this refute the cause and effect of the Mahāyāna?
Answer: You state that the diamond-like mind (*vajracitta*) is the impermanent stage of saṃsāra, whereas the subsequent mind is the permanent stage of the fruit of Buddhahood, which is nirvāṇa.
Birth and death are exhausted before; the fruit of Buddhahood arises after.
When the cause ceases, there is no fruit before;
when the fruit arises, there is no cause after.
How could this be a matter of cause and effect?
Since cause and effect are not established, you are merely destroying the Triple Gem yourself;
how does it concern me that I am destroying anything?
He asked again, "Are cause and effect definitely two distinct things?
He replied, "If the cause is impermanent, how could it be the effect?
If the effect is permanent, how could it be the cause?"
If that is so, the Sūtra says:
"For those who possess duality, there is neither the Path nor the fruit.
[Question: The Sūtra says:
By practicing the causes, one attains the fruit of Bodhi.
Having attained that fruit, one subsequently enters the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) to teach and transform sentient beings.
How could it be said that this does not exist?
Answer: A bodhisattva does not take up the fruit by means of practicing the cause;
rather, it is solely for the purpose of guiding sentient beings.
Thus, at midnight, he leaped over the city walls and renounced desire, merely to awaken them to the realization that nothing truly exists.
Regarding the Bodhisattva, one has never said that there is birth-and-death,
nor has one said that there is nirvana,
nor has one said that there is a cause.
Nor does it say that there is a fruit;
these two [distinctions] are merely opened up for the sake of teaching and transforming sentient beings.
Furthermore, you ask: "Do you attain bodhi by practicing causes?"
Is it that the ultimate fruit is attained, or is it not attained?
If it were attained, it would be eternal; if it were not attained, it would be annihilated.
In either case, there would be neither cause nor effect.
Furthermore, at what time is bodhi cause and effect?
It is not that a non-cause is metaphorically designated as "cause," nor that a non-effect is metaphorically designated as "effect."
Nor are there four or five; it is not that because there are no fruits called "four" or "five" that they are designated as such.
Therefore, it is simply called "fivefold enlightenment."
Because "shallow" and "deep" are provisional designations for what is shallow and deep,
the arousal of the thought of enlightenment (bodhicitta) is considered shallow and the Buddha is considered deep.
Furthermore, the four [bodhisattva stages] are the cause, while the Buddha is the fruit.
Although you exert diligent effort, this is the second [point] refuting cause and effect:
it clarifies that while you claim an ordinary person attains the fruit of Buddhahood by cultivating causes,
at the time one is an ordinary person, Buddhahood does not yet exist.
At the time of the Buddha, there are no longer ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). If it were certain that there were no Buddhas during the time of being an ordinary being,
then even though one were to practice with diligence, one would ultimately never attain Buddhahood.
Because one cannot attain certainty regarding the non-existence of a Buddha, nor attain certainty regarding the non-existence of a Buddha,
one will ultimately never become a Buddha.
Furthermore, this is the Mahāyāna method for refuting the meaning of the Hīnayāna.
The Mahāyāna clarifies that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and shall all attain Buddhahood;
those of the Hīnayāna do not clarify that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
If that were so, since there would be no Buddha-nature, one would never become a Buddha despite practicing cultivation.
Question: The followers of the Hīnayāna also say this.
All sentient beings possess the natures of the three vehicles.
Upon reaching the stage of the Dharma of Patience (*kṣānti*), the other two natures cease to be subject to analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*).
Therefore, within the three vehicles, one establishes oneself in whichever single vehicle is appropriate.
Why is it said that the Buddha-nature is not clearly explained?
The answer is: within the Mahāyāna, it is clearly taught that there is only the Buddha-nature and no other nature;
therefore, one attains Buddhahood.
If the Hinayana does not clarify that there is only Buddha-nature,
it subverts the Mahayana doctrine of Buddha-nature; and since the Mahayana Buddha-nature would then be non-existent, [the teaching of liberation would be undermined].
How does one attain Buddhahood?
Furthermore, those of the Hīnayāna possess Buddha-nature;
this [assertion] that Buddha-nature is impermanent subverts the Mahāyāna principle that Buddha-nature is eternal.
Therefore, one cannot attain Buddhahood.
This verse explains the text of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*;
thus, it should not be said that it merely expounds upon the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
Furthermore, based on the text, this verse is explained as follows:
Those of the Hīnayāna claim that the natures of the six realms of existence are eternally not the Buddha-nature;
here, "nature" (xing) refers to the essence (ti).
Therefore, the bodies of ordinary beings and sages are distinct.
If this is so, they are neither identical nor definitively different.
How then can it be established that [the Buddha] has not attained [this]?
"Is it that everyone who attains this becomes a sage?
He asked again, "Do those of the Mahāyāna, who clearly possess the Buddha-nature, attain Buddhahood?"
Answer: The interpretations of Buddhahood by those who grasp at attainment in the Mahāyāna are all invalid.
For example, although there are ten different schools that interpret Buddhahood, they all claim that Buddhahood is definitively eternal.
They merely appear to be different; however,
since both sentient beings and the mind are all impermanent,
the mind and sentient beings are never, at any time, the Buddha-nature.
How is Buddhahood attained?
If all phenomena were not empty, it would lead to the second fault: the negation of both demerit and merit.
Furthermore, this is divided into two distinct parts.
The first clarifies the absence of the causes and effects of sin and merit;
the second clarifies the absence of conventional phenomena,
which corresponds respectively to the former two points.
The first section consists of two parts:
the former clarifies that there is no person who creates sin or merit;
the latter two verses clarify that there is no dharma of sin or merit.
Now, the discussion of sin and merit does not transcend the categories of person and dharma.
Since these do not exist, how can there be sin and merit? You say:
I teach that in emptiness, no one can kill;
there is neither one who kills nor an object to be killed, and because there are no swords or staves, there is no transgression.
Furthermore, there is neither one who gives nor one to whom a gift is given.
Furthermore, because there are no entities, there is no merit.
If you now possessed a fixed nature such that the killer, the killed, and the sword or staff each abide in their own nature and cannot move, [then killing would be impossible].
Therefore, there is no transgression.
Since each abides in its own nature, neither can one give nor is there merit.
This second section, situated within the discussion of transgression and merit, clarifies the dharma that is devoid of both transgression and merit.
The two verses constitute two parts:
the first clarifies that when cause and effect are separated, there is neither sin nor merit;
the second clarifies that even when cause and effect are not separated, there is likewise neither sin nor merit.
All that constitutes sin or merit does not transcend these two;
since these two do not exist, one knows they are non-existent.
The first half of the initial verse restates this.
To say "unborn" means that what has not yet arisen is simply unborn.
The second half [of the verse] refutes the notion that the fruit exists within the causes of demerit and merit;
if it did, then cause and effect would be separate from one another.
How can a cause produce an effect? Furthermore,
because outsiders (bāhyaka) cling to the existence of a fixed nature (svabhāva),
karmic retribution ought not to arise from demerit or merit.
If [retribution] does not arise from sin or merit,
then there would be a karmic result independent of sin and merit;
such is the meaning of the verse.
The second verse directly clarifies that cause and effect are not separate:
since the effect exists by virtue of the cause, yet the effect lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
the effect is therefore empty.
Because the effect exists, the cause is also empty.
Furthermore, these two verses are explained by means of two refutations:
as for your statement that there are fruits of sin and merit, [it is refuted as follows].
Does the fruit arise from a cause, or does it arise without a cause?
The first verse refutes the latter;
the second verse refutes the former.
Regarding your refutation of all phenomena, the second section below addresses the fault of returning to the conventional.
This consists of three verses divided into two parts:
the first verse serves as the general statement, and the latter two as the specific analysis.
The verse is easy to understand.
Now I ask about another point:
you maintain that cause and effect exist in the conventional sense (*saṃvṛti*).
If true non-existence were the cause and effect,
then one side would exist while the other side would not.
One part is negated while another part is not.
If one speaks of the ultimate truth, then the causes and effects of the conventional truth are negated.
To speak of the conventional world while destroying the ultimate truth results in the non-existence of cause and effect.
If both the principles of cause and effect and the absence of cause and effect were to coexist, they would be like two horns,
or like lines drawn upon stone.
If the ultimate and the conventional were mixed into a single entity, both truths would be lost.
Having refuted the meaning of emptiness, the second section specifically clarifies the absence of the conventional.
The first verse clarifies that there is no essence to persons or phenomena.
The subsequent verse loses the characteristic of all things;
within conventional phenomena, the essential nature does not emerge.
Furthermore, the first verse is free from the fault of artificial construction.
The subsequent verse contains the fallacy of eternalism;
the verse is easy to understand.
Now, I shall inquire into the meaning of the other [position].
If you claim that although the cause lacks the fruit, the cause clearly produces the fruit,
then you must be transforming non-existence into existence,
such as taking a rabbit’s horn to be a cow’s horn.
If one does not take non-existence as existence, then one takes existence as existence.
Since it already exists,
what need is there to bring it into existence?
Just as that which already exists as a cause should not further function as a cause,
why should that which already exists as a fruit need to arise again?
Furthermore, if a cause were without a fruit, it could not produce existence.
Form should become mind, and mind should become form;
the permanent should become impermanent, and the impermanent should become permanent;
if existence were to act upon existence, then once it has already existed...
What need is there to act?
Thus, that which is non-existent does not become existent; that which is existent does not become existent.
Furthermore, that which is both existent and non-existent does not become existent.
Furthermore, you claim that from the impermanence of saṃsāra one produces the permanence of the Buddha-fruit;
yet if so, the permanence of the Buddha-fruit should likewise produce the impermanence of saṃsāra.
If this were not the case, would it not follow that there is a fixed nature?
He asked me: "The dharmas of humans are conventionally existent according to worldly truth;
when, then, do they possess intrinsic nature?"
I ask you: Is this name merely conventional, or does it exist as a reality?
If it exists as a reality, is this not a fixed nature?
If one says that because a nature cannot be found, can one then falsely construct the meaning of "non-falsity"?
The next verse clarifies the absence of marks (*animitta*),
as the text explains.
If there were no emptiness, the Master would provide a third summary of his response in the subsequent commentary to admonish and exhort;
since this chapter thoroughly refutes both the mundane and the supramundane,
it is necessary to clarify these admonitions and exhortations.
Furthermore, gain and loss are matters of great significance.
As it says in the *Prajñāpāramitā*:
"The *prajñā* arises for the sake of a great matter."
That is to say, it demonstrates what is the path and what is not the path;
now it is likewise:
it demonstrates that there is a determinate nature to be attained, and this is not the path.
To demonstrate that the causes and conditions for non-attainment are what is called the Path,
the subsequent section clarifies admonition and exhortation;
the preceding verse clarified the admonition.
The following verse clarifies the exhortation.
The preceding verse cautioned against clinging to any determinate nature in that which is apprehended;
if you persist in grasping at a determinate nature, you shall not attain anything, whether mundane or supramundane.
Since nothing that is lost is truly lost,
one should abandon the notion of intrinsic nature;
this is because the verse speaks of a fixed nature.
Therefore, that which has not yet been attained cannot be obtained, nor can afflictions be severed or suffering brought to an end.
The following verse exhorts one to study the causes and conditions for attaining everything. "All that is to be attained..."
Regarding "those who lose everything":
this verse briefly clarifies that seeing the causes and conditions results in two kinds of benefits.
First, seeing a person is seeing the Buddha.
Next, it clarifies that seeing the Dharma is seeing the Four Noble Truths.
The long discourse states:
To see the causes and conditions is to see the Dharmakāya;
causes and conditions are themselves the nature of quiescence.
This nature of quiescence transcends the four propositions and surpasses the hundred negations.
Therefore, in the Tathāgata-parivarta, quiescent extinction is taken as the Dharma-body.
Furthermore, the very sixteen-foot [form] is itself the Dharma-body;
thus, although he is sixteen feet tall, his crown cannot be seen.
How could that which is below be definitively low?
If one says it is high, then how can it be only sixteen feet?
Therefore, we know this.
It is neither high nor low, neither finite nor infinite.
Thus Master Zhao said:
"How could one abandon the sixteen-foot form and seek the Dharma-body from afar?"
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:
"This body of mine is itself the Dharma-body.
Question: When perceiving causes and conditions, one perceives only the Dharma-body.
One also sees the response-body (nirmāṇakāya).
Answer: Seeing that the causes and conditions are quiescent is seeing the dharma-body (dharmakāya);
seeing the quiescence of causes and conditions is seeing the response-body.
If one clearly perceives the meaning of the three bodies, one sees the seven-foot body as embodying the three bodies.
The seven-foot body is fundamentally quiescent, which is the Dharma-body;
seeing the Dharma-body and being in accord with the Dharma-body is the Sambhogakāya (Response Body).
Yet, since these seven feet remain as they were, this is indeed the Nirmāṇakāya (Transformation Body).

Those who perceive the Four Noble Truths see the causes and conditions of cessation; seeing suffering and its origin, they see the causes and conditions of cessation—that is, they see cessation and the path.
In the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, it is said that to see dependent origination is to see the Dharma;
to see the Dharma is to see the Buddha;
and to see the Buddha is to see the Buddha-nature.
This is precisely what is cited in the present treatise.
Question: For what reason does the author of the treatise clarify the seeing of causes and conditions?
Answer: One must understand the general purport of this treatise as well as the great tenets of the Buddha-dharma.
This is the correct refutation of intrinsic nature and the presentation of causes and conditions.
Having completed the refutation above that intrinsic nature exists and is empty of intrinsic nature,
we now present the existence of causes and conditions.
Since that which exists through causes and conditions is ultimately empty,
it is therefore empty of causes and conditions.
One should take this as the correct meaning.
Chapter 25: Nirvāṇa (10a–10b). Chapter Twenty-Five: Nirvāṇa. Question: For what reason is nirvāṇa refuted immediately following the Chapter on the Four Noble Truths?
Answer: Both the Great and Small Vehicles possess four truths and one truth.
The Small Vehicle elucidates the four truths of the finite;
its ultimate tenet rests upon the single Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).
The Mahāyāna speaks of four immeasurables,
yet its ultimate tenet also returns to the single Truth of Cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The reason why both the Great and Small Vehicles ultimately return to the single Truth of Cessation is as follows:
The three truths are all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*);
only this cessation (*nirodha*) is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and eternally abiding.
Furthermore, because this cessation is the ultimate fruit, being final and without remainder.
The three truths converge upon this single ultimate;
therefore, having previously refuted the four truths, one now contemplates nirvana.
Furthermore, it is by receiving the teaching of the four truths that understanding is born.
Because one attains nirvana by severing the afflictions (*kleśa*),
one first contemplates the Four Noble Truths and subsequently contemplates nirvana.
Furthermore, the author of the *Satyasiddhi-śāstra* says:
The equality of the Four Noble Truths is itself nirvāṇa.
This teaching is extensively contained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*.
Therefore, what was explained above—that the emptiness of the Four Noble Truths is precisely what is meant by emptiness as nirvāṇa—is established.
Therefore, this present chapter fully clarifies that none of the four positions constitute *nirvāṇa*.
How, then, can emptiness (*śūnyatā*) be taken as *nirvāṇa*?
Question: For what reason is *nirvāṇa* refuted at the very end of the twenty-five chapters?
Answer: The outsider claims that nirvana is the fundamental abode for settling the spirit, the common destination for both ordinary beings and sages.
Thus, Master Zhao said:
"At this point, the nine schools all converge."
The multitude of sages thus meet in profound harmony.
Various Vaipulya sutras also extensively discourse on this teaching;
therefore, the Lotus Sutra says:
Ultimate nirvana is the mark of eternal quiescence, ultimately returning to emptiness;
therefore, the final discussion concerns nirvana.
Second is the general meaning of the Buddha’s appearance in the world.
It is for the sake of causing sentient beings to abandon birth and death and attain Great Nirvana.
If this were so, there would necessarily be birth and death to be abandoned and nirvana to be attained.
This principle is unerring.
Because it is definitively existent, it is discussed last.
Third, the external refers to:
Nāgārjuna appeared in the world and composed treatises to refute erroneous views and elucidate the great essentials of the sūtras;
he also enabled sentient beings to escape the suffering of birth and death and attain nirvāṇa.
If it were not for the purpose of liberating beings from the suffering of birth and death and enabling them to attain nirvana,
for what reason would one refute [erroneous views regarding] illness and proclaim the Buddha’s teaching? Therefore,
we know that the ultimate aim of composing this treatise is nirvana.
Therefore, it is the final treatise.
According to the sūtras, since the Buddha preached his final nirvāṇa at the twin śāla trees,
this is the final treatise of the Master.
The different interpretations of *nirvāṇa* are explained:
the seven views of the non-Buddhist teachers, the two theories of the Hīnayāna, and the four reckonings of the Vaipulya.
Regarding the seven views of the non-Buddhist teachers, the first maintains that *nirvāṇa* is no different from the absence of afflictions (*kleśa*).
Second, they reckon that nirvāṇa is the cause of the absence of afflictions;
third, they establish that nirvāṇa is the fruit of the absence of afflictions;
fourth, they clarify that ultimate non-existence is what is called nirvāṇa.
This is as explained in the "Chapter on Refuting Permanence" (*Nityatva-parihāra*) of the *Śata-śāstra*.
Next, the Brahmin Dantika maintains that this very body is itself nirvāṇa and need not be further extinguished;
this clarifies that he regards the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) as nirvāṇa.
Next, Ārāḍa Kālāma reckoned non-perception to be nirvāṇa;
this reckoning takes the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*) to be nirvāṇa.
Udraka Rāmaputra reckoned the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) to be nirvāṇa.
This [view] considers the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) to be nirvana.
These three non-Buddhists take the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) as nirvana;
together with the preceding [four], they constitute seven types [of views].
Regarding the two masters of the Hīnayāna:
the first, the Abhidharmika, maintains that unconditioned nirvāṇa is eternal and wholesome;
it exists inherently from the beginning, outside of the afflictions.
Subsequently, when the afflictions are severed, the arising of the "attainment of attainment" (prāpti-prāpti) belongs to the practitioner.
Second, the *Tattvasiddhi* clarifies that nirvāṇa is merely a non-existent dharma (abhāva-dharma) and is not subsumed under the three natures (tri-svabhāva).
That which is obtained from wholesome causes is explained as being wholesome.
Regarding the four kinds [of the Mahāyāna]:
the first clarifies that the essential nature of *nirvāṇa* is a phenomenon of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The reason for this is that by refining minor wisdom, one ultimately achieves great enlightenment.
There is no accumulation of defilements that is not stilled, and no virtue that is not perfected.
Therefore, Nirvana is called an existent dharma (*dharmasat*).
The second explanation states:
Taking emptiness as nirvana is precisely the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa).
The true nature (dharmatā) is called the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya).
The third explanation states:
Nirvāṇa is neither real nor conventional.
Conventional truth is coarse existence;
ultimate truth is wondrous non-existence.
Nirvana is distinct from that coarse existence.
Furthermore, it is not the same as the wondrous non-existence;
therefore, it lies outside the two truths.
The fourth explanation states:
Within the four propositions, it is not that one reaches the ultimate by transcending these four propositions that constitutes *nirvāṇa*.
It is simply that the four masters differ in their great elucidation of two types.
According to the *Tattvasiddhi*, it clarifies that there are two types of *nirvāṇa*: the fundamental and the initial.
The Master of the Ten Stages clarifies both the purity of nature (*prakṛti-viśuddhi*) and the purity of expedient means (*upāya-viśuddhi*).
The purity of expedient means is that which is attained by cultivating causes;
the purity of nature, however, has existed eternally throughout past and present.
However, "purity through expedient means" (upāya-viśuddhi) is merely another name for that which first comes into being,
whereas "purity by nature" (prakṛti-viśuddhi) is a distinct designation for that which is originally present.
This is as explained in the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* regarding the four kinds of nirvāṇa.
First, the quiescence of intrinsic nature;
second, with remainder;
third, without remainder.
